consensus_summary: The lion’s primary and most characteristic Christian meaning is Christ as the conquering ‘Lion of the tribe of Judah,’ embodying royal power, majesty, strength and victory (Rev 5:5; Gen 49:9-10); it is simultaneously recognized as a polyvalent symbol whose context can yield Satan the devourer, divine judgment, hostile empires/rulers, or generic courage.
book_summary: The lion is a royal and devouring ruler or empire: wicked rulers (Assyria, Babylon, Israelite princes) bear the predatory figure, while its rightful holder is the Lion of Judah.
consensus_core_identification: Christ the messianic Lion of Judah (royal/sovereign power), set within an explicitly polyvalent field that also includes predatory evil and earthly powers.
book_core_identification: A royal and devouring ruler or empire, whether wicked (Assyria, Babylon, etc.) or rightful (Lion of Judah).
boundary_disagreement: Book restricts the symbol to rulers/empires (positive and negative) and does not treat Satan, pure divine wrath, generic courage of the righteous, or the evangelist Mark as proper referents.
rationale: Both readings share the same biblical cluster (Lion of Judah + predatory kings/empires). The consensus treats the Christological sense as primary and the imperial/wicked-ruler sense as one common alternative among several; the book elevates the ‘royal devouring ruler/empire’ category itself to the core identification and subordinates Christ to the status of its ‘rightful holder.’ This preserves the central royal-power referent while materially narrowing the extension and re-ranking the cases, producing a refinement rather than equivalence or contradiction.
strongest_objection: Consensus uniformly ranks the Christological Lion of Judah as the primary meaning, not merely the rightful instance of a more general ‘ruler/empire’ figure.
